To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the seismoelectric response is a complex signal that can provide information about the interface between two media, and that this information can be used to infer the characteristics of the interface.

(i) seismoelectric signals can be detected in boreholes penetrating an aquifer; (ii) the polarity of these signals is related to the vertical extent of the source zone below the interface; and (iii) the maximum amplitude of the seismoelectric signal is influenced by partially cemented layers at the water table. [2]

the seismoelectric signal at the water table is generated by a combination of the growth of the source zone, the maximum vertical extent of the source zone below the interface, and the presence of partially cemented layers that straddle the interface.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of seismoelectric methods as an aid to hydrogeophysical characterization of aquifers.

the development of a new geophysical method, seismoelectric geophysics, for mapping the water table and the subsurface distribution of water saturation in unconsolidated sediments and fractured rocks.
the development of a conceptual model for the seismoelectric effect at the water table.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

these measurements are the first to demonstrate that the interfacial seismoelectric signal is sensitive to the vertical extent of a partially cemented layer and the growth rate of a partially cement layer below the water table. [2]

the interfacial conversion is a result of the interaction of the seismic waves with the interface and its properties, and that the amplitude of the seismoelectric signal depends on the seismic energy that propagates through the water-saturated layer.

the seismoelectric effect at an interface can be modeled as a source of electric current that is proportional to the product of the seismic wave velocity and the seismic wave particle velocity, and that the source is confined in space to a region of maximum thickness equal to the wavelength of the seismic wave.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
seismoelectric signals can be measured and used to characterize interfaces and the physical properties of porous media.
seismoelectric methods can provide information on the location and geometry of the water table, as well as the presence of partially cemented layers in unconsolidated aquifers. [2]
seismoelectric methods have the potential to provide new information about the structure and dynamics of aquifers. [2]
The main takeaway from our work is that
seismoelectricity is a powerful tool that can be used to characterize aquifers and their boundaries.
the seismoelectric effect is sensitive to the presence of partially cemented layers in an otherwise homogeneous aquifer.
the polarity of seismoelectric signals can be used to infer the growth rate of source zones below the water table and the maximum vertical extent of the source zone below the interface.
